verses.translation_literal: And Jacob settled in the land of the sojournings of his father, in the land of Canaan.
verses.translation_dramatic: So Jacob settled. He sat down at last in the country where his father had only ever been a guest, among the same hills and wells and borrowed pasture: the land of Canaan. Esau's line had been counted off, chief by chief, in a mountain of its own. Jacob took no deed to anything. He took the long patience of the sojourner, and stayed.
verses.directors_commentary:
Chapter 36 has just closed on Esau: his chiefs listed one by one, settled in Seir, in "the land of their possession" (36:43). Then one verse, and the camera swings to Jacob. The verb is plain, "sat, settled", but the place is "the land of his father's sojournings", and *megurim* is the vocabulary of the resident alien, the *ger*, who lives on land that is not his by the courtesy of those who own it. Abraham and Isaac grazed by treaty and dug wells under dispute; Jacob inherits their status without their title. Ramban hears the contrast on purpose: Esau's chiefs held land outright, while Jacob sat as a guest in the land that was promised but not yet given.

The KJV ("wherein his father was a stranger") turns the noun into a relative clause and loses the plural, a whole life of tent-pitching in one word. The BBE ("had made a place for himself") says almost the opposite of the Hebrew. The verse ends by repeating "in the land of" and naming Canaan last, as if the whole family history were walking toward that word. Rashi reads the quiet opening as a signal: Genesis hurries through Esau and slows down for the line that matters.

philological_notes.note: "Sojournings of": the plural of *magor*, from the root *gur*, to live as a resident alien without land rights (the same root as *ger*). It marks the Patriarchs' status in Canaan: present, but as guests.
"Sat, settled." The same verb as Esau's settling in Seir, set here against a land that is not owned. The contrast with ch. 36 is the point of the opening.

verses.translation_literal: These [are] the generations of Jacob: Joseph, a son of seventeen years, was shepherding with his brothers among the flock; and he [was] a youth with the sons of Bilhah and with the sons of Zilpah, the wives of his father; and Joseph brought their evil report to their father.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is what came of Jacob: not a list of names, but a boy. Joseph, seventeen years old, out on the hills with his brothers and the flock, a youth among the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph carried tales. He carried them home, and laid their ugly report before their father.
verses.directors_commentary:
"These are the *toledot* of Jacob" is the formula that heads every major section of Genesis, and it is normally followed by a genealogy. Here no list comes. Radak and Ibn Ezra read *toledot* as "what was born of him", the events that came out of Jacob's life as a day gives birth to its happenings (Prov 27:1), and that is truer to the story than the KJV's "generations". The generation that follows is told through one son.

The syntax is knotted. *Et* means both "with" and the object marker, so Sforno hears "he was shepherding his brothers", as their guide; Radak, noting "among the flock" has no article, hears a learner who walks along. *Na'ar* is "youth" but also "junior attendant": Joseph is the youngest hand among the sons of the secondary wives. The KJV calls him "the lad" and makes his place in the party vague. "Wives" here, though 35:22 calls Bilhah a *pilegesh*: Ramban takes it as the narrator's courtesy once Rachel and Leah are dead.

Then the report. *Dibbah* is a whispered word of ill repute, the noun used for the spies' slander of the land (Num 14:36). The Hebrew never says what Joseph reported, or whether it was true or whose behaviour it was. Rashi supplies three sins (eating a limb from a living animal, calling the maidservants' sons slaves, sexual misconduct); Ramban asks why the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah would not protect him; Sforno says it was bad herding. All of that is commentary. The text gives only the act: the youngest hand reports on his elders to their father.

philological_notes.note: "Generations" in the sense of what is begotten, and so of what a life produces: events. Here the formula opens a narrative, not a genealogy.
"Youth", "attendant". Ramban notes that Scripture uses it for men of forty (Rehoboam) and for Absalom, so it describes rank and subordinate position more than age. Seventeen is no child.
A whispered report, a rumour; the Hebrew does not say whether it was true. Rashi ties it to *dovev siftei yeshenim* (Song 7:10), speech that murmurs on the lips.

verses.translation_literal: And Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, for he [was] a son of old-ages to him; and he made for him a tunic of pasim.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Israel loved Joseph. He loved him more than all his sons, because Joseph was the child of his old age, and the old man could not hide what his heart had chosen. He had a tunic made for him, a tunic of *pasim*, a garment that spoke before its wearer did.
verses.directors_commentary:
The narrator switches from "Jacob" (vv. 1-2) to "Israel", the name of the father who loves, the patriarch with his authority and his blindness. Whether the shift is deliberate or only the narrator's variation, here it names Jacob in his role as head of a household and giver of favour.

"Son of old age" is an odd phrase for Joseph, since Jacob's sons were all born within some seven years (Radak raises the objection). So the commentators go in two ways. Onkelos reads "a wise son" (*bar chakkim*), a son with an old man's judgment; Ramban reads it as the son kept close to attend an aging father. The plural *zekunim* is an abstract ("old-ages"), and later Benjamin is "child of old age" in his turn (44:20), so it names a relation more than a birth order.

The tunic is the verse's famous crux. The KJV's "coat of many colours" comes from the old Greek and Latin renderings (as I recall it, a "variegated" garment), not from the Hebrew, where *pas* is the "palm, sole, extremity": a tunic reaching to the extremities, long to the wrists and ankles (YLT, BBE: "long"), or striped or panelled (Radak). Rashi links it with the royal tunic Tamar wore (2 Sam 13:18). Either way it is a garment of rank for someone who does not do field work, and the rabbis knew it: for the sake of a few shekels of extra fine wool, Radak quotes, the brothers' envy took the family to Egypt (Shabbat 10b). The verb "and he made" is a perfect with *vav*, not the narrative form: it may well be "he had made", a gift already given and worn before the dreams begin.

philological_notes.note: "Son of old-ages": either a child born late (Ibn Ezra, 91 years old at Joseph's birth), a wise child with an old man's insight (Onkelos, Radak), or one kept at hand to attend an old man (Ramban). Ramban prefers the last.

The root *pas* means palm or sole, so a tunic reaching the palms and soles, or striped, or ornamented. Ibn Ezra compares Daniel 5:5 (*pas yada*, the palm of a hand). The STEPBible gloss "palms and soles" is the root meaning; the sense of the garment is still debated.

verses.translation_literal: And his brothers saw that it was him their father loved more than all his brothers, and they hated him; and they were not able to speak to him for peace.
verses.translation_dramatic: They saw it. It was him their father loved, above all his brothers. And they hated him. They could not make their mouths say even one word of *shalom* to him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is built on a hinge: "loved" and "hated" are set one after the other (*ahav* ... *vayisne'u*), and the whole feud is that one inversion. Note the fronted "him" (*oto*): not "that their father loved Joseph", but "that it was HIM he loved". The brothers are looking at a verdict, not a fact. And "more than all his brothers" is in their voice, "his brothers", the brothers of the favoured one, reading him from their side of the family.

The last clause is sharper than the English. *Lo yakhelu* is "they were not able", not "they would not": the BBE turns an inability into a refusal. And what they cannot do is *daber lashalom*, speak a word of *shalom*, the daily greeting. Rashi turns this to their credit: from their fault we learn their virtue, for they said nothing with the mouth that they did not mean in the heart. The KJV's "speak peaceably" is reasonable English, but it loses that the word in question is a greeting: this is a household where nobody says good morning. Sforno puts the blame on Jacob, who made the difference between the sons visible when he need not have.

philological_notes.note: "For peace": *shalom* is the greeting and the state of well-being. Not to speak it is to withhold the minimum courtesy. Rashi reads the failure as a kind of honesty: they spoke nothing false.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph dreamed a dream and told [it] to his brothers; and they added still to hate him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it to his brothers. And what they felt, which had seemed full already, was added to.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs carry the verse and both are loaded. *Vayyagged*, "and he told", is the plain word for reporting; the next verse, with *shim'u na*, shows how Joseph tells it. And the brothers "added" to their hatred: *vayyosifu*, from *yasaf*, "to add". It is the root of Joseph's own name (*Yosef*, Gen 30:24, "may he add"). The brothers' hatred is a growing sum, and the Hebrew makes the child's name the unit of increase. The KJV's "yet the more" is fine English, but the name-play is lost in every English version. It returns in v. 8.

Radak notes why the dream is told at all: telling it was a way of hurting them, given how much they envied him for his father's love. Sforno takes it kindly and says it was a boy's lack of judgment. The text gives neither. We get only the sequence: dream, report, more hatred. Dreams were taken as messages from the gods in the ancient Near East; hearing one told by the favoured son was never neutral.

philological_notes.note: "And they added": from *yasaf*, the root behind the name Joseph (*Yosef*, Gen 30:24). The verb recurs in v. 8, so the narrator hangs the brothers' hatred on the hero's name. An observation about the text; no source.

verses.translation_literal: And he said to them, "Hear, please, this dream that I dreamed."
verses.translation_dramatic: "Listen," he said to them. "Please. Listen to this dream I dreamed."
verses.directors_commentary:
A short verse that does a great deal. The politeness is in the Hebrew (*na*, "please"), and the trouble is the same politeness: it asks for an audience from people who cannot say *shalom* to him. The command *shim'u* is the formal word for "hear" (the same verb as *Shema*), which makes the announcement a summons. Sforno hears it as more than a story: "understand what this dream means". The brothers answer him exactly that way in v. 8: they decode it at once.

The KJV's "I pray you" is the old way to render *na*; today it reads as pompous, and it shifts the tone to churchy. In modern speech the line is a youth's eager, slightly breathless "listen to this".

verses.translation_literal: "And behold, we [were] sheaving sheaves in the middle of the field, and behold, my sheaf rose and also stood upright; and behold, your sheaves gathered round and bowed down to my sheaf."
verses.translation_dramatic: "There we were, binding sheaves in the middle of the field, and look: my sheaf rose up. It stood upright. And look: your sheaves came gathering round it, and they bowed down to my sheaf."
verses.directors_commentary:
Three times "behold" (*hinneh*) pulls the listener inside the dream, as the dreamer saw it: *we* were binding, *my* sheaf, *your* sheaves. The pronouns are the whole drama. The sound carries the sense as well: *me'allemim alummim*, a verb made from the noun, "sheaving sheaves", and the *-im / -ah* endings roll through the sentence like stalks in wind. The KJV's "binding sheaves" keeps the sense and drops that echo.

The verbs build upward: *qamah*, rose; *nitzavah*, stood upright; then the others *tesubbeinah*, circled round. Ramban sees in the circling the court of a king, with servants camped around him. The brothers' answer in v. 8 shows that is how they heard it. And the dream is farmers' work: a field, a harvest, the late spring grain cut and bound in handfuls, which shows that the herding clan also sowed and reaped. Radak points out how neatly the dream fits later events, when grain brings the brothers to bow before Joseph in Egypt. The KJV's "made obeisance" is Jacobean for the same verb as v. 9 and v. 10, *hishtachavah*, to bow low to the ground.

philological_notes.note: A verb formed from the noun *alummah* (sheaf), "to sheave". Onkelos translates "to bind bundles" (*me'assrin esarin*); Ibn Ezra relates it to the noun *alummim*, also found in Ps 126:6.
"They gathered round": the root *savav* is to turn, circle. Ramban hears a king surrounded by his attendants.

verses.translation_literal: And his brothers said to him, "Reigning, will you reign over us? Or ruling, will you rule over us?" And they added still to hate him, for his dreams and for his words.
verses.translation_dramatic: His brothers answered him: "You? Reign over us? You, rule over us?" And their hatred was added to again, for his dreams and for his words.
verses.directors_commentary:
They read the dream in a single breath, and what they read is kingship. Each question is a verb doubled by its own infinitive (*hamalokh timlokh*, *mashol timshol*): "Reigning, will you reign?" The Hebrew infinitive absolute makes the question a mocking intensity. The KJV catches it ("shalt thou indeed reign ... shalt thou indeed have dominion"), as does YLT. The BBE flattens it. The two verbs, *malakh* (to be king) and *mashal* (to rule), are not quite the same: Onkelos and Ramban take it that he could not be either one to them, neither king nor governor. The brothers, who live in a world of city-kings, know exactly what "reign" means.

And again "they added" (*vayyosifu*), the Joseph-root of v. 5. The reason is given twice: "for his dreams", plural, though one dream has been told (Radak asks whether he had others), "and for his words". Rashi hears "his words" as the old tale-telling of v. 2; Ramban and Sforno hear the telling of the dream itself, the "listen!" of v. 6. I follow the second reading, but the Hebrew *devarav* leaves both open.

philological_notes.note: The infinitive absolute with the finite verb gives emphasis, "Will you indeed reign?", and with the interrogative *ha* a taunt. Ramban notes the pair of verbs (*melekh* and *moshel*) as two ranks that Joseph will never hold over them.
"His dreams", plural, although only one has been told. Radak: perhaps an earlier dream, or the plural is generic for this one and the next.

verses.translation_literal: And he dreamed again another dream, and recounted it to his brothers; and he said, "Behold, I have dreamed a dream again, and behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars [were] bowing down to me."
verses.translation_dramatic: And Joseph dreamed again, another dream, and he told it, too, to his brothers. "Look," he said, "I have dreamed one more dream. The sun and the moon and eleven stars were bowing down to me."
verses.directors_commentary:
The second dream goes up from the field to the sky. The sun and moon are not only family images here: in Egypt's religion the sun is Re, in Mesopotamia Shamash and the moon Sin, and the heavenly bodies are gods. A dream where they bow is a dream that turns the world's order over. Radak and the commentators read the sun and moon as parents and the eleven stars as the eleven brothers (Joseph is the twelfth, which is why he is not counted).

The verb is a participle, *mishtachavim*, "were bowing down": not one act of homage but a continuing scene, in which the obeisance does not end. Both dreams use the same verb *hishtachavah*, which the KJV renders "made obeisance", the posture of the whole body prostrate that later becomes the court gesture the brothers will make in Egypt. Note the number "eleven" is without the article in Hebrew; the KJV's "the eleven stars" makes them a known set, whereas the Hebrew simply counts them: eleven stars. There is also a different verb for telling: *vayesaper* (recount, the root of "number" and "scribe"), in place of v. 5's plain *vayyagged*. This time he tells it as a full account.

philological_notes.note: "Bowing down": the *hishtaphel* of *shachah*, to bow low, prostrate oneself, whether to a king or to a god. A participle, so the scene goes on.
Sun and moon. Radak: the parents. Ramban (on v. 10) reads the moon as Jacob's whole household of wives, because Rachel was already dead.

verses.translation_literal: And he recounted [it] to his father and to his brothers; and his father rebuked him and said to him, "What [is] this dream that you dreamed? Coming, shall we come, I and your mother and your brothers, to bow down to you, to the ground?"
verses.translation_dramatic: He told it to his father, and to his brothers. And his father rebuked him. "What is this dream you have dreamed?" he said. "Shall we come, I and your mother and your brothers, and bow down to you, down to the ground?"
verses.directors_commentary:
This time Joseph tells it to his father with the brothers there (Rashi: after telling the brothers, he told it again before them to Jacob), and now the sun is Jacob himself, and the father does the decoding. He reacts with *ga'ar*, the verb of a sharp rebuke (it is also God's "rebuke" of the sea). The question is the same form as the brothers' in v. 8: *havo navo*, "Coming, shall we come?", and Jacob unpacks the dream into its actors: "I, your mother, your brothers". The KJV's "come to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth" follows the Hebrew closely and loses only the contempt of *mah*, "what ...?"

The problem is "your mother", and every commentator sees it: Rachel died on the road to Ephrath (35:19). Rashi reads Jacob as using the impossibility to talk himself and his sons out of the dream: if this part cannot happen, none of it needs to. Ibn Ezra says the sun's partner is Bilhah, who raised Joseph. Ramban prefers to take the moon as the wives collectively. Whichever, the father publicly cuts his favourite down in front of the brothers, which may calm them (Ramban), and v. 11 will show that his heart did not agree with his mouth. *Artzah*, "to the ground", is the posture of the full prostration, which Joseph's brothers will perform before him in Egypt, as Ramban notes citing 43:26.

philological_notes.note: "Rebuked": a strong word for a rebuke or threat. Ibn Ezra distinguishes *ga'ar* with the preposition *bet* (rebuke with disgrace) from the bare form (destroy, Mal 2:3).

"And your mother": Rachel was dead (35:19). Rashi and Radak read the impossibility as proof the whole dream is empty talk; Ibn Ezra takes it as Bilhah, who raised him; Ramban reads the moon as the household.

verses.translation_literal: And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the word.
verses.translation_dramatic: His brothers were consumed with jealousy of him. But his father kept the word, and kept it close.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two reactions set side by side, with the same subject. The brothers are *vayqan'u*, "jealous, zealous", an outward, burning passion (the root also used of God's own zeal). The father *shamar*, "guarded, kept", the verb for a watchman or a shepherd's care. He has just rebuked the boy aloud, yet he does not let the matter drop. The Hebrew *davar* means both "word" and "thing, matter". In v. 8 the brothers hated Joseph for his *devarav*, "his words"; here the father keeps the *davar*. The same noun marks both reactions: the sons hate the speaker for his words, the father keeps the word itself. The KJV's "observed the saying" is archaic: "observed" in 1611 can mean "kept", but a modern reader hears "noticed". BBE's "kept his words in mind" is closer.

How the father kept it is debated. Ibn Ezra and Radak: in his heart, though he rebuked it aloud, he could not wave it away. Rashi: he waited and watched for it to come. Sforno adds that he half hoped it would be true. Rashbam says the line explains Jacob's later belief in Joseph's survival, when the wagons arrive from Pharaoh, so the father who keeps this word is also the one who will know what it means.

philological_notes.note: "Kept, guarded": Rashi takes it as watching and waiting for the thing to arrive, citing Isaiah 26 and Job 14. Ibn Ezra: kept in the heart.
"The word / the matter": the same noun as the brothers' hated *devarav* in v. 8.

verses.translation_literal: And his brothers went to pasture (*et*, dotted) the flock of their father at Shechem.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then his brothers went away to pasture their father's flock at Shechem. Shechem: a name with an old memory in it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene breaks: the dreamer is left with his father and the brothers go off with the flock. The narrator opens the new scene by naming the place, and the place is Shechem, where Simeon and Levi had slaughtered the men of the city after the rape of Dinah (Gen 34). Radak notes that the brothers were not afraid to go back: the terror of God had fallen on the cities around them, and time had made the thing seem forgotten. The reader remembers it better than they do.

The Masoretes put dots over the word *et* in this verse (the *puncta extraordinaria*, visible in the Hebrew above). Those dots mark a word suspect or to be read with care. Rashi and Radak, from the Midrash, read the dots as a hint that "they went not to pasture the flock, but to pasture themselves", with *et* (the sign of the object) read as "themselves": they went to eat and drink at their own pleasure, far from their father. This is a derash, a rabbinic reading of the dots, not what the sentence says. KJV's "feed" for *lir'ot* is also a little off: *ra'ah* is to pasture, to shepherd, the same verb as Joseph's in v. 2, which makes these brothers the shepherds and Joseph the youth.

philological_notes.note: The word is dotted in the Masoretic text. Rashi, from the Midrash, takes the dots as saying they went to pasture themselves and not the flock.

verses.translation_literal: And Israel said to Joseph, "Are not your brothers pasturing at Shechem? Come, and I will send you to them." And he said to him, "Here I [am]."
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Israel said to Joseph, "Your brothers: are they not out pasturing at Shechem? Come. I will send you to them." And the answer came in a single word, hineni: "Here I am."
verses.directors_commentary:
The old man's question ("Are not your brothers pasturing...?") assumes what both of them know and neither says: the brothers are far away, in the one district of Canaan with a bloody history for this family (Gen 34). Rashbam says outright that Shechem was dangerous, a place where the family had killed the men of the city. Sforno asks the practical question: is it not a long way? Radak's reading is that Jacob does not suspect harm, or he would not send him, and that the whole episode is arranged by God so that the family should go down to Egypt.

The father is again "Israel", the name of the head of the house with his authority, and his "Come, and I will send you" is the language of a man giving a commission. Joseph's answer is a single word, *hineni*, "here I am", the readiness answer that Abraham gave God at 22:1 and 22:7. The KJV renders it with the same "Here am I"; what it cannot show is that the answer is complete: no question, no objection. Rashi hears humility and eagerness in it, a son who hurries to do his father's will even though he knows his brothers hate him.

philological_notes.note: "Here I am": the answer of one who presents himself ready to a superior, as Abraham did at 22:1. Rashi reads it as humility and zeal; Radak says Joseph feared nothing because he trusted his father's authority over the brothers.

verses.translation_literal: And he said to him, "Go, please; see the shalom of your brothers and the shalom of the flock, and bring me back a word." And he sent him from the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Go," his father said. "Please. See the peace of your brothers, and the peace of the flock, and bring me back word." So he sent him out of the valley of Hebron, and Joseph came to Shechem.
verses.directors_commentary:
Look at the word the father chooses: *shalom*, twice. "See the *shalom* of your brothers, the *shalom* of the flock." Four verses ago the narrator told us that the brothers could not speak *shalom* to Joseph (v. 4). Jacob is sending the one son who gets no greeting to inquire after the well-being of the ones who cannot give it. The KJV ("see whether it be well with thy brethren, and well with the flocks") and the BBE turn *shalom* into a phrase and hide the repetition. The Hebrew also says "bring me back a *davar*", a word, a report. The noun recalls v. 8, where the brothers hated Joseph for his *devarav*, "his words", and v. 11, where the father "kept the *davar*". Verse 2 is a thematic echo only: there Joseph brought their *dibbah*, "report", a different noun. The son who once brought a bad report is now sent for a report.

The geography is a long walk. Hebron lies in the hills, and the Hebrew calls it *emeq*, a valley. Rashi quotes the Midrash that this is a hint at the "deep counsel" made with Abraham, who is buried at Hebron, that his seed would be strangers (Gen 15:13). Hebron to Shechem is some eighty kilometres as the crow flies, three days on foot; Dothan lies about twenty-three kilometres further. Ramban draws the moral: the text names the starting point to show how far the brothers were from their father, and how far Joseph went out of respect for him.

philological_notes.note: "Welfare, peace", twice. Echoes the brothers' failure to speak *shalom* to Joseph (v. 4). Radak, quoting Genesis Rabbah, draws from the second use that one must ask after the welfare of what one profits from, here the flock.

"From the valley of Hebron". Hebron is on high ground, which puzzles Rashi; he gives the Midrash on "deep counsel" (*etzah amukah*), a wordplay on *emek*. Radak adds that Jacob went with Joseph down to the valley and sent him from there.

verses.translation_literal: And a man found him, and behold, he [was] wandering in the open country; and the man asked him, saying, "What are you seeking?"
verses.translation_dramatic: And a man found him. There was Joseph, wandering in the open country, going this way and that, and the man asked, "What are you looking for?"
verses.directors_commentary:
A tiny scene with a large mechanism. The text gives the stranger no name, no origin, no reason to be there, and he is the hinge of the story: without him Joseph turns back from an empty Shechem and nothing happens. The tradition cannot leave him unexplained. Rashi, following the Midrash, makes him the angel Gabriel, from Daniel 9:21, where Gabriel is "the man"; Pseudo-Jonathan agrees. Ramban explains why: a long account of Joseph's trouble in finding his brothers shows that the plan of God stands, and that Joseph's own diligence is empty without it. Ibn Ezra, with *peshat*, says only that he was a passerby. I follow the plain sense in the dramatic layer and leave the angel to the commentary.

The verb "wander" (*ta'ah*) is the one used of straying from the road, and the KJV's "a certain man" adds a word the Hebrew does not have: it is just "a man". The BBE says he "saw" him, but the verb is *matza*, "found". Joseph is lost, and someone finds him. Rashbam draws the point that matters for the character: Joseph, not finding them at Shechem, does not go home, though he knew they hated him; he searches until he finds them, because his father had said to bring back word. His question, "what are you seeking?", is also a question about the whole story, as Sforno senses ("you are not going straight").

philological_notes.note: "Wandering, straying", off the road. Ramban takes it as literally lost, searching the grazing land because that is where flocks are. Radak: going back and forth looking for them.
"A man", unnamed. Rashi: Gabriel (Dan 9:21). Ibn Ezra: a passerby. Ramban: a guide sent by God without Joseph's knowing.

verses.translation_literal: And he said, "My brothers I [am] seeking. Tell me, please, where they [are] pasturing."
verses.translation_dramatic: "My brothers," he said. "It is my brothers I am looking for. Tell me, please: where are they pasturing?"
verses.directors_commentary: The Hebrew puts the object first: *et achai anokhi mevaqqesh*, "My brothers, I am seeking". It is the only answer Joseph gives, and it names the very people we know to hate him. The English "I seek my brethren" (KJV) flattens the emphasis, and the old *thee/thou* and "I pray thee" makes the boy sound like a priest. The point is the simplicity: an errand, a destination, a polite "please" (*na*) to a stranger. He asks "where are they pasturing", repeating the word of his father's question (v. 13) so that the whole conversation hangs on one verb. Radak and Ibn Ezra add "if you know" to the request. Sforno hears a request for the exact stretch of grazing land. Nothing in the verse suggests fear; for the reader, who has just seen "my brothers" given the weight of a verdict, everything in it does.

verses.translation_literal: And the man said, "They have set out from here, for I heard [them] saying, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" And Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
verses.translation_dramatic: "They have gone from here," the man said. "I heard them say, Let us go to Dothan." And Joseph went after his brothers, and he found them at Dothan.
verses.directors_commentary:
The man's reply is oddly shaped: not "they are at Dothan" but "they have set out from here, for I heard them say, Let us go to Dothan". He knows only what he overheard. Ramban notes the oddity and uses it to explain the Midrash, which finds a double meaning in the man's words. Rashi hears a pun in the place name *Dotayna*: it sounds like *datot*, laws or pretexts, so "let us go to Dothan" is read as "let us go and look for legal pretexts to put you to death". Rashi adds at once that the plain sense is a place name. Ibn Ezra notes that the spelling with a yod and without it is the same place, and Rashbam says the plain sense is the city's name and that it is mentioned elsewhere too; his text names Judges, which I could not confirm (the registry places Dothan from Gen 37:17 to 2 Kings, where it is the town of Elisha's story, 2 Kgs 6).

*Nase'u*, "they have set out", is the verb for breaking camp, and Sforno reads it as a statement that the group has moved on from this stretch of pasture. The direction ending on *Dotayna* ("toward Dothan") means the trip is a leg beyond Shechem. Dothan, a fertile valley on the route toward the Jezreel Valley and the coastal road, was the kind of place where caravans passed, which the next verses will need. The KJV's "departed hence" is archaic for "gone from here". Sforno adds a detail about Joseph's loyalty: though he did not find them as his father said, he took more trouble than he was told to.

philological_notes.note: "To Dothan": a place name with the directional ending. Rashi plays on *datot* (pretexts, laws): they went to find ways to kill him. He then adds that the plain sense is the place name.
"They have set out, pulled up": the verb for breaking camp. Sforno: they left this grazing ground and one need not look for them in it.

verses.translation_literal: And they saw him from afar, and before he drew near to them, they schemed against him to kill him.
verses.translation_dramatic: They saw him from far off: one figure on the path, coming nearer. And before he drew near to them, they had schemed against him. To kill him.
verses.directors_commentary:
Everything in the verse happens in the gap between "afar" and "near": they see him, they plot, and he has not yet arrived. The verb is *vayitnakkelu*, in the reflexive intensive form (*hitpael*) of *nakhal*, "to act craftily, to deal deceitfully". Rashi: they were "filled with cunning". Sforno notes it means to picture a thing in one's mind, as in 1 Sam 28:9 and Numbers 25:18, where *nikhlu* is the verb for the Midianites' seduction of Israel. The KJV's "conspired" and the BBE's "made a secret design" both carry the sense of planning but lose the connotation of guile. And the last word, *lahamito*, "to kill him", is stated flatly: the Hebrew does not wrap it.

Why could they see him "from afar"? In open country, with no cover and a clear day, a walker is visible for kilometres. It is also possible, and this is my own reading and not in the commentaries, that the long tunic of v. 3, now on the road, was what made him recognisable at a distance. Ramban adds a darker reading: that they had already tried to kill him by some trick before he arrived (the Midrash has them setting dogs on him), and, failing, said to each other, "he is coming, let us kill him ourselves." Radak notes the odd grammar of "scheme [with] him": the object marker is used as "to" or "with", "against".

philological_notes.note: "They schemed": *hitpael* of *nakhal*, to deal craftily; the same root as *nekhel*, scheme, in Num 25:18. Rashi, Rashbam and Ibn Ezra take it as plotting with cunning; Sforno as picturing the evil in the mind.

verses.translation_literal: And they said, a man to his brother, "Behold, the master of the dreams, this [one], is coming."
verses.translation_dramatic: They said it to one another, a man to his brother: "Look. Here he comes, the master of dreams."
verses.directors_commentary:
*Ba'al hachalomot*, "master of the dreams": *ba'al* is "owner, lord, possessor", the word for a husband (a woman's *ba'al*) and the name of the storm god of Canaan. Said of a man, it is a taunt: the lord and owner of dreams, the dream-merchant. The KJV's "this dreamer" and the BBE's "this dreamer" keep the contempt but lose the grandeur they are mocking, the title of a lord. It is a title they give him instead of a name; he is no longer their brother. And *hallazeh*, "that one over there", is the demonstrative for someone seen at a distance (Rashbam: you say *hallazeh* of someone far off and *hazzeh* of someone near), so the word itself still has the "afar" of v. 18 in it.

The idiom *ish el achiv*, "a man to his brother", is the standard Hebrew way to say "to each other", but here the word "brother" is a bitter one: every man in that circle is the brother of the man he is plotting against. Sforno reads the whole phrase as a complaint: he told us the dreams only to provoke us into sinning against God or our father, and so to be destroyed.

philological_notes.note: "Master of the dreams": *ba'al* means owner, master; it is also the Canaanite god's name. A sarcastic title rather than the neutral "dreamer". Onkelos has *mare chelmaya*, "lord of dreams", close to the Hebrew.
"That one": the demonstrative for someone far off. Rashbam sets it against *hazzeh* for what is near.

verses.translation_literal: "And now, come, and let us kill him, and let us throw him into one of the pits, and we shall say, 'An evil beast has eaten him'; and we shall see what will become of his dreams."
verses.translation_dramatic: "Now then. Come. Let us kill him, and throw him into one of the pits, and we will say, A wild beast has devoured him. And then we shall see what becomes of his dreams."
verses.directors_commentary:
Four cohortatives in one sentence (kill him, throw him, say, see) make a plan with the shape of a plan: act, hide, explain, wait. *Lekhu*, "come", is the call that summons people to a joint act (Rashbam compares "come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites"). They speak of "one of the pits", and the cisterns around a grazing camp are numerous, since the whole economy of a pastoral district in a dry land depends on stored water. "An evil beast" (*chayyah ra'ah*) hands Jacob the very words he will say himself in v. 33; the adjective *ra'ah* is the same as the "evil report" Joseph brought in v. 2. The KJV's "some evil beast" and "some pit" add an indefinite *some* the Hebrew lacks, and the BBE's "holes" are cisterns.

The last clause is the one the tradition cannot leave alone. *Venir'eh mah yihyu chalomotav*: "and let us see what will become of his dreams". Ramban reads it as mockery: let us see whether we bow to him after he is dead. Sforno: we will see the dreams exposed as false. Rashi, quoting a rabbi, hears the Holy Spirit in the sentence: they say "kill him" and the text ends "we shall see whose word will stand", theirs or God's. The brothers' sentence and its ironic reading are both in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: "And let us see what will become of his dreams." Ramban: a taunt. Sforno: the dreams will be shown false. Rashi (citing a rabbi): the Holy Spirit's ironic reading, whose word will stand.
"Come": an invitation to a joint act. Rashbam compares "come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites" (v. 27); Sforno: hurry and agree to kill him.

verses.translation_literal: And Reuben heard, and rescued him from their hand, and said, "Let us not strike him [to the] life."
verses.translation_dramatic: But Reuben heard. And Reuben took Joseph out of their hands. "We will not strike at his life," he said.
verses.directors_commentary:
The firstborn speaks. The verbs rush: he *heard*, he *rescued*, he *said*. The rescue is stated first and the speech afterwards, because the speech is the rescue; Joseph is still out of sight, and it is the brothers' hands that Reuben is pulling him out of. Hebrew *yad*, "hand", will keep returning (v. 21 "from their hand", v. 22 "a hand do not send", v. 22 "from their hand"); it is the word for power, for violence, and, ironically, for the thing that the brothers will manage to avoid.

The idiom *lo nakkenu nafesh* is literally "let us not strike him [as to] life", an accusative of limitation: don't strike at the life. The KJV ("Let us not kill him") and the BBE state the result; the Hebrew states the blow. Rashi and Radak gloss it as "a deadly blow"; Ibn Ezra compares Exodus 33:11, where Joshua is a *na'ar*, with the abstract meaning of the noun. Sforno reads Reuben's rescue with a pang: even a righteous man falls once, and Reuben's own sin with Bilhah (Gen 35:22; 49:4) is the shadow behind this attempt to make good with his father.

philological_notes.note: "Let us not strike him [to the] life": *nefesh* as an accusative of limitation, "a blow to the life", a mortal blow. Ibn Ezra cites the pattern of Exodus 33:11.

verses.translation_literal: And Reuben said to them, "Do not shed blood. Throw him into this pit that [is] in the wilderness, and a hand do not send against him"; so as to rescue him from their hand, to return him to his father.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Shed no blood," Reuben told them. "Throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him." He meant to rescue Joseph out of their hands, and to give him back to his father.
verses.directors_commentary:
Reuben argues with the brothers' own words. They said *nashlikhehu*, "let us throw him" (v. 20); he says *hashlikhu*, "throw him", but into a pit and alive. Where they said "kill", he says "shed no blood" (*dam*, which carries the guilt of blood), and "send no hand" (*yad al tishlechu*), the Hebrew for "lay no hand". The verb *shalakh* (throw) will occur a third time when they act on his version (v. 24). His wording is careful: he does not say "his blood". Ramban reads this as Reuben presenting himself (*hereh atzmo*) as sharing their hatred, so as not to seem to speak from love for Joseph; he asks only that they not shed blood with their own hands. Ramban closes that Reuben's intent throughout was to rescue Joseph and return him to his father. The *peshat* is that the pit is a death sentence by exposure; only the narrator, in the purpose clause, tells us the true intent: Reuben meant to save him and "return him to his father".

That last clause is a rare moment of access to a character's secret: the narrator steps in to testify. Rashi: the Holy Spirit testifies for Reuben, who wanted to come back and pull him out, saying "I am the firstborn; the blame will fall on me." "The wilderness" (*midbar*) is not desert but open, uncultivated land used for grazing, and "this pit" means a well-known one, near at hand. The KJV's "wilderness" can mislead a modern reader, but it follows the Hebrew; the KJV reproduces *shed no blood* and *lay no hand* almost exactly. Its "that he might rid him out of their hands" is a heavy way of saying "to rescue".

philological_notes.note: "Do not shed blood": the language of murder guilt. Reuben does not say "his blood". Ramban: Reuben presents himself as sharing their hatred and objects only to shedding blood with their hands, while his real aim was to rescue Joseph and return him to his father; Radak: it is innocent blood, since Joseph has done nothing worthy of death.
"So as to rescue": the narrator's purpose clause, giving Reuben's secret intent. Rashi: the Holy Spirit testifies to it. Rashbam: the end of the story proves it.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, when Joseph came to his brothers, that they stripped Joseph of his tunic, the tunic of the pasim that [was] on him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And it happened. Joseph came to his brothers, and they stripped him, stripped Joseph of his tunic: the tunic of *pasim* that he wore.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse piles up its objects: "they stripped *Joseph* [*et*] *his tunic* [*et*] *the tunic of the pasim* that was on him". Three object markers (*et*) in a row, as if the brothers were pulling the garment off in stages. The repetition of "tunic" and the repeated name are not padding: the name of the coat is the grievance. Radak says the second phrase names the coat because "over it they were jealous"; Rashbam adds that the coat is named here so that the scene of the bloodied coat in v. 32 reads as a deception. For Rashi it is simply the extra his father gave him over his brothers. The KJV repeats "coat of many colours" for the tunic here, with the same problem as in v. 3.

Ibn Ezra notes the verb *hifshit* takes two objects, the person and the garment, and that the *ketonet* is the garment next to the skin: they stripped it, and the Hebrew implies the boy was thrown into the pit naked. That reading ("they tricked him, and threw him naked into the pit") is Ibn Ezra's, not the Hebrew's, which says only "stripped". The act is also a ritual of humiliation and of disinheritance: to take off a man's mark of rank is to take it away. And the garment is kept: it has a purpose in v. 31.

philological_notes.note: "They stripped": a verb that takes the person and the garment as two objects. Ibn Ezra notes this and the implication that Joseph was thrown into the pit naked.

"The tunic of the pasim", the full name, repeated from v. 3. The second naming after "his tunic" is explained by Radak (the reason for their jealousy) and by Rashbam (the tunic is mentioned in order to be used in the deception).

verses.translation_literal: And they took him and threw him [to] the pit; and the pit [was] empty, there was no water in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: They took him. They threw him into the pit. And the pit was empty; there was no water in it.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three short actions: take, throw, look. The camera then turns to the pit itself, with two statements that repeat each other: "empty", and "no water in it". The second does not repeat the first, say the rabbis. Rashi, quoting the Talmud (Shabbat 22a): "empty" would not have told us it had no water, so "no water in it" is added to teach that there was no water, but there were snakes and scorpions. Rashbam and Radak take it as the plain sense that water would have drowned him, which would have made the brothers killers; Reuben's "lay no hand" shows why it matters that the pit be dry. In the autumn, at the end of the rainless summer, cisterns are low or dry, as the story needs. The KJV keeps the doubled statement ("the pit was empty, there was no water in it").

The verb "throw" (*vayashlikhu*) comes for the third time in the chapter (vv. 20, 22, 24): the plan, the amendment, and the deed. The Hebrew *hab-borah* has the directional ending, "toward the pit". Radak notes the oddity of "they took him" (*vayyiqqachuhu*) written without a vav, and quotes Genesis Rabbah that this was Simeon, the one whom Joseph will later take and bind in Egypt (42:24). The word *bor* will return as the name of Joseph's Egyptian prison (40:15): first a pit for a brother, then a pit for a slave.

philological_notes.note: "Empty": Rashi (citing Shabbat 22a) says the added "no water" implies snakes and scorpions. Radak asks whether it might hold mud, as in Jeremiah 38:6. Ramban says on the plain sense that a little water would still be "empty".

verses.translation_literal: And they sat down to eat bread, and they lifted up their eyes and saw, and behold, a caravan of Ishmaelites [was] coming from Gilead, and their camels [were] carrying spice-gum (*nekhot*) and balm and ladanum (*lot*), going to take [it] down to Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: And they sat down to eat bread. The boy lay in the pit, and they sat down to eat bread. Then they lifted up their eyes, and saw: a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels loaded with gum and balm and ladanum, on the road down to Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The most chilling clause in the chapter is the first: they sat down to eat. Rashbam pictures them a little away from the pit, so as not to "eat over the blood"; Sforno, with a harder eye, says that a true righteous man whose act had gone wrong would have fasted, as Israel did at Bethel in Judges 21 and as Darius did when Daniel went into the lions' den. These men had decided Joseph was a pursuer (*rodef*) whose death was justified, so they could sit and eat. The KJV's "sat down to eat bread" keeps this; "bread" (*lechem*) is the Hebrew word for a meal.

The next phrase, "lifted up their eyes and saw, and behold", is the narrator's formula for a sudden sighting, the same formula as Abraham spotting the ram at 22:13 (my observation). The caravan carries gum, balm and ladanum, aromatic resins from Gilead's hills that were sold in Egypt for incense, perfume, embalming and medicine; the balm of Gilead becomes proverbial in Jeremiah 8:22, as Ibn Ezra notes. Their identities are disputed: Rashi explains *nekhot* as a mix of spices, Onkelos and the Midrash as wax or gum; *tzori* as resin from the balsam tree (Rashi, Radak) and *lot* as ladanum or a root (Rashi). The KJV's "spicery and balm and myrrh" is a fair guess, but *lot* is not myrrh as a rule. Rashi asks why the Torah lists the cargo: normally Arabs carry smelly naphtha and tar; a sweet-smelling load was arranged for the righteous Joseph. Finally, the verb *lehorid*, "to take down", is the same root (*yarad*) that Jacob will use of himself in v. 35: Joseph goes down to Egypt, Jacob swears he will go down to Sheol, and later the whole family goes down.

philological_notes.note: A spice or aromatic gum, exact identity uncertain. Rashi: any collection of spices; Onkelos and Radak (citing Genesis Rabbah): wax; Ibn Ezra links it with *bet nekhot* in 2 Kings 20:13, the treasure house.
Probably ladanum, a resin; Rashi gives a root (Mishnaic *lotita*), Radak (citing Genesis Rabbah) another plant name. STEPBible's 'myrrh' follows the KJV tradition.
"To take down": causative of *yarad*. The same root recurs in Jacob's 'I will go down' (v. 35). An observation about the text.

verses.translation_literal: And Judah said to his brothers, "What profit [is it] if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?"
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Judah spoke to his brothers. "What do we gain," he said, "if we kill our brother and hide his blood?"
verses.directors_commentary:
Judah argues like a merchant. *Betza* is "gain, profit", and it often means gain made by violence: Ibn Ezra cites Psalm 30:10, "What profit is there in my blood?" The word is a bitter irony, because the "profit" he finds is in selling Joseph (v. 27); the silver itself is named only in v. 28. The KJV's "What profit is it" is right; BBE's "covering up his blood" is equally right.

The second verb, "conceal his blood", is both a practical and a moral problem. The practical sense, which Ramban prefers, is the plain one: murderers bury the body and cover the blood with earth (compare Moses and the Egyptian, Exod 2:12). The moral sense: in Genesis blood does not stay covered, as Cain learned when Abel's blood cried from the ground (4:10); Rashi and Radak read it as hiding the death from their father. Ramban catches the legal point: Reuben had said no blood be shed by their hands, and Judah now says that leaving Joseph to die in a pit would count as killing him anyway. Sforno hears a calculation of honour and fear of the father. Judah says "our brother" (*achinu*) and not "Joseph" or "the dreamer", the first of the brothers in the scene to call Joseph "our brother". (In v. 19 *ish el achiv* means each man to his brother, not a name for Joseph.)

philological_notes.note: "What profit": *betza* is gain, often ill-gotten. Ibn Ezra compares Ps 30:10; Rashi and Onkelos translate 'what money'. Sforno: vengeance has no use if it pains ourselves and cannot warn others, since we would hide it.
"And we conceal his blood": Rashi and Onkelos take it as hiding his death; Ramban reads it literally as burying the blood in the ground, as murderers did.

verses.translation_literal: "Come, and let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and our hand, let it not be on him; for he [is] our brother, our flesh." And his brothers listened.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Come. Let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let our hand not be on him. He is our brother, after all, our own flesh." And his brothers listened.
verses.directors_commentary:
"Come" (*lekhu*) is the same summons as in v. 20, but with the verb changed from *nahargehu* ("let us kill him") to *nimkerenu* ("let us sell him"). "Let our hand not be on him" echoes Reuben's *yad al tishlechu bo* in v. 22 almost exactly. Judah is working with the words already on the table. And "our brother, our flesh" is the language of kinship (compare Adam's "flesh of my flesh", 2:23, and Laban's "my bone and my flesh", 29:14). What the brothers do not see, or say, is that selling a man was itself a death-penalty offence in the later law, "he who steals a man and sells him shall be put to death" (Exod 21:16), which is why they can hold both thoughts in mind only by treating "hand" as the only offence.

*Vayishme'u*, "they listened", means in Hebrew that they accepted and obeyed; Rashi gives the rule: when "hear" means accepting words, Onkelos translates *qibbel* "accepted", when it means the ear's hearing, *shema'*. The KJV's "were content" and the ASV's "hearkened" are both fair. Sforno hears measure for measure: the one who would rule them becomes a slave.

philological_notes.note: "Let our hand not be on him": avoiding direct violence. It repeats Reuben's formula in v. 22. Radak: so as not to cause his death, as selling him would not.
"They listened", in the sense of accepting. Rashi sorts the two senses of the verb, and Onkelos renders this one *qibbel*.

verses.translation_literal: And men, Midianites, traders, passed by; and they drew and brought up Joseph from the pit, and they sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty of silver; and they brought Joseph to Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then men passed by: Midianites, traders. And they drew Joseph up out of the pit, and they sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. And they carried Joseph to Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse that decides who sold Joseph does not say. Its verbs are all third-person plural with no new subject: they passed, they drew, they brought up, they sold, they brought. The reader has three choices. Rashbam: Midianite traders happen by, find Joseph in the pit, pull him up and sell him to the Ishmaelites while the brothers sit eating at a distance; later "you sold me" (45:4) holds because their deed brought it about. Rashi: three or four sales, brothers to Ishmaelites to Midianites to Egyptians. Radak and Ibn Ezra: the Midianites and Ishmaelites are one caravan under two names, as in Judges 8:24, so the brothers drew him up and sold him. Ramban separates the caravan owners (Midianite merchants) from the camel-drivers (Ishmaelites). I kept the Hebrew's ambiguity in the literal layer and, in the dramatic layer, the same flat grammar.

Two more features. Joseph's name is repeated three times in one verse ("drew Joseph... sold Joseph... brought Joseph"), the Hebrew's way of making a person an object passed from hand to hand. And the KJV's "twenty pieces of silver" adds "pieces": the Hebrew is "twenty of silver", a weight of uncoined metal, around 230 grams, since coined money does not exist yet. In Leviticus 27:5 twenty shekels is the valuation of a boy aged five to twenty. The Midrash's Pseudo-Jonathan has the brothers buy sandals with the price.

philological_notes.note: Midianites, descendants of Midian son of Keturah. Radak and Ibn Ezra identify them with the Ishmaelites (compare Judges 8:24); Ramban separates them as owners and camel-hirers.
"For twenty [of] silver": a weight of silver (shekels, understood). The KJV supplies 'pieces'.

verses.translation_literal: And Reuben returned to the pit, and behold, Joseph [was] not in the pit; and he tore his clothes.
verses.translation_dramatic: Reuben went back to the pit. And behold: Joseph was not in the pit. And he tore his clothes.
verses.directors_commentary:
Where had Reuben been? The text does not say, and the commentators fill the gap: Rashi gives the Midrash that it was his turn to go and serve his father; or, in another account, that he was busy with sackcloth and fasting for having disordered his father's bed (35:22). Radak says he had been somewhere with the flocks, and returned to the pit to take Joseph out secretly. The Hebrew only says that he "returned" (*vayyashov*), the verb that will mean his plan: to bring the boy back (*lehashivo*) to his father (v. 22).

His reaction is physical: *vayyiqra et begadav*, he tore his clothes, the standard gesture of grief and horror. It is the first of three tearings in the chapter: Reuben tears his own clothes (v. 29), Jacob tears his (v. 34), and between them the brothers have torn Joseph's off him. The KJV's "rent" is archaic; the BBE's "giving signs of grief" is vague. The "behold" (*vehinneh*) puts the reader inside Reuben's eyes, as we were in Joseph's dream: *ein Yosef babbor*, "no Joseph in the pit". The Hebrew *ein*, "there is not", is the word that will become the family's refrain for him (v. 30, and 42:36).

philological_notes.note: "He returned", to the pit. Radak: he went back hoping to take Joseph out without his brothers knowing and return him to his father.

verses.translation_literal: And he returned to his brothers and said, "The boy [is] not; and I, where am I going?"
verses.translation_dramatic: He went back to his brothers. "The boy is gone," he said. "And I? Where do I go now?"
verses.directors_commentary:
A short cry with a double *I*: *va'ani, anah ani va*, "and I, where do I go?" Ibn Ezra notes the pronoun is said twice and calls it rhetoric. It is a firstborn's cry: he was to answer to his father for the boy. Rashi hears: "where can I flee from my father's grief?" Rashbam: "why did I come to the pit?" Radak: Reuben did not know of the sale; he thought the boy had been stolen from the pit.

*Hayeled*, "the boy, the child": Joseph is seventeen (v. 2) and was *na'ar* (youth); Reuben calls him *yeled*, the word for a small child, the language of protective tenderness. The KJV and ASV's "child" catches it. *Einennu*, "he is not", is the word Jacob will use of Joseph in 42:36 ("Joseph is not, and Simeon is not"), which is the family's code word for what has happened. The BBE "the child is gone; what am I to do?" is a paraphrase that makes the second clause a practical question; the Hebrew is the more helpless "where do I go?"

philological_notes.note: "And I, where am I going?": the pronoun is doubled for emphasis (Ibn Ezra). Rashi: where can I flee from my father's grief?

verses.translation_literal: And they took the tunic of Joseph, and they slaughtered a he-goat of the goats, and they dipped the tunic in the blood.
verses.translation_dramatic: They took Joseph's tunic. They slaughtered a he-goat, and dipped the tunic in its blood.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three brisk verbs, and a cover story is made out of a household's herd. *Vayishchatu*, "they slaughtered", is the word for slaughter of animals for food or sacrifice; they butcher the goat as they would for a meal. Rashi and Radak, from the Midrash, note that goat's blood resembles human blood. The KJV's "a kid of the goats" is off: *se'ir izzim* is a "hairy" he-goat, a full-grown male, not a young *gedi* (kid); the ASV's "he-goat" is correct. The tunic is now *hakkutonet*, "the tunic"; Rashi notes that the noun is pointed *kutonet* on its own and *ketonet* when joined to another word, as in "tunic of Joseph" and "tunic of the pasim".

The goat is also an irony the commentators do not mention: Jacob once deceived his blind father with the skins of two *gedi'ei izzim*, kids of the goats (27:9, 16). Now his sons deceive him with a goat, and the deceiver is deceived (my observation).

philological_notes.note: "A he-goat of the goats": *sa'ir* is the shaggy male goat. The KJV's 'kid' is wrong; 'kid' is *gedi*. Rashi and Radak, citing the Midrash: its blood looks like a man's.

verses.translation_literal: And they sent the tunic of the pasim, and they brought [it] to their father, and they said, "This we found; recognise, please: [is] it the tunic of your son, or not?"
verses.translation_dramatic: They sent the tunic of pasim, and they had it brought to their father. "This we found," they said. "Look at it, please. Is it your son's tunic, or not?"
verses.directors_commentary:
The brothers do not come themselves. *Vayshalechu*: "they sent", and Rashbam says they sent it by other people so that no one could say who the senders were. Ramban lists the options: through messengers while still at Dothan, or to Hebron with a messenger who said "we found this", all to avoid Jacob suspecting them, since he knew their jealousy. Another reading takes *vayshalechu* as "they ripped it" with a blade (*shelach*), to make it look torn by animals (Ramban, Radak, Sforno).

The wording is the genius of the lie. They never say Joseph is dead; they say only "we found", and ask a question: *haker-na*, "recognise, please". They do not say "our brother" but "your son" (*binkha*), as far from the "our brother, our flesh" of v. 27 as they can get. The verb *nakar* (to recognise) is the one that will turn on them: in 38:25 Tamar says to Judah the same *haker-na*, which Radak draws from Genesis Rabbah; and in 42:8 Joseph recognises his brothers and they do not recognise him (my observation). The KJV's "know now whether it be thy son's coat or no" is a little stiff and repeats "coat of many colours"; the Hebrew is a short, flat request to identify an object.

philological_notes.note: "Recognise, please": the verb of identification. Radak, citing Genesis Rabbah, links it with Tamar's *haker-na* to Judah (38:25): Judah's own words come back to him.
"They sent": Rashbam and Ramban, through others so they could not be questioned; another reading, in Ramban, Radak and Sforno, derives it from *shelach* (blade) and has them tear the tunic.

verses.translation_literal: And he recognised it and said, "The tunic of my son! An evil beast has eaten him; torn, torn [is] Joseph."
verses.translation_dramatic: He knew it at once. "My son's tunic," he said. "A wild beast has devoured him. Torn, torn to pieces is Joseph."
verses.directors_commentary:
Look at what the brothers did not say. They asked only whether he knew the tunic. Jacob answers with the sentence they had planned in v. 20, word for word: *chayyah ra'ah akhalatehu*, "an evil beast has eaten him". They never spoke it to him; he says it himself. The lie is completed by its victim, and the brothers' hands stay clean of a spoken falsehood. It is also what the Midrash calls the Holy Spirit flashing within him (Rashi: *chayyah ra'ah*, the wild beast, as Potiphar's wife, who will go after Joseph in ch. 39), but Jacob does not know what he said.

The last clause is a cry: the infinitive absolute, *taroph toraf*, "torn, torn", the same emphatic doubling that the brothers used in v. 8 ("reigning, will you reign") but now in grief; the KJV's "without doubt rent in pieces" is a stiff English for a sob. Ibn Ezra notes the form (*toraf* is a passive with no stated agent). Jacob identifies the tunic as "the tunic of my son", not Joseph's name, until the very last word. The garment he gave as a mark of love is now the only proof that love is lost. The KJV's "It is my son's coat" turns the exclamation into a statement.

philological_notes.note: "An evil beast has eaten him": the exact words planned in v. 20. Rashi, citing the Midrash: the Holy Spirit stirred in Jacob, and the beast is Potiphar's wife.
"Torn, torn": an infinitive absolute with a passive verb. Ibn Ezra explains the form: the agent is not named, and the spelling avoids doubling the *resh*.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob tore his garments, and put sackcloth on his loins, and mourned for his son days many.
verses.translation_dramatic: Jacob tore his clothes. He put sackcloth about his loins. And he mourned for his son, many days.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three rites in order: tear the outer garment, bind on sackcloth, mourn. The *simlah* he tears is the large outer cloak; the *sak* is a coarse cloth, usually goat's hair, worn at the loins (Sforno: a belt of the cloth from which sacks are made). This is the full mourning costume of the Near East: the clothes that show rank are destroyed, and the body is clothed in the same material as bags. The name is again "Jacob", the grieving man, the deceiver deceived. The KJV's "rent" and "loins" are accurate; the BBE's "haircloth" and "giving signs of grief" smooth the details.

"Many days" (*yamim rabbim*) is the Hebrew idiom for an unspecified but long time. Rashi counts twenty-two years, from Joseph's disappearance to Jacob's arrival in Egypt, balanced against the twenty-two years in which Jacob did not honour his own parents (Meg. 16b). That is the tradition's reading; the plain sense is weeks or months of acute mourning, and the later lines (v. 35) show a grief that has no end. Radak adds a layer of guilt: Jacob sent him alone, and thought himself to blame.

philological_notes.note: "Many days": unspecified long time. Rashi counts 22 years, the span to Jacob's descent into Egypt, in return for the 22 years in which Jacob did not honour his parents.
"Sackcloth": coarse cloth, the mourner's garment worn at the loins. Sforno: a belt made of the weave from which sacks were made.

verses.translation_literal: And all his sons and all his daughters rose to comfort him, and he refused to be comforted; and he said, "For I will go down to my son mourning, to Sheol." And his father wept for him.
verses.translation_dramatic: All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, and he would not be comforted. "No," he said, "I will go down to my son, mourning, to Sheol." And his father wept for him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The family circle forms around the old man and fails. "Rose" (*vayyaqumu*) is the gesture of a household coming to the mourner. "All his daughters" puzzles the commentators, since only Dinah is known. Rashi and Radak give the Midrash: twin sisters born with each tribe, or, in the other opinion, daughters-in-law, since people call a son-in-law "son" and a daughter-in-law "daughter"; Ramban compares Naomi's "my daughters" to Ruth and Orpah. *Vayema'en lehitnachem*: "he refused to be comforted". Rashi quotes the Midrash: no one accepts consolation for someone alive whom he thinks dead, because the decree on the dead is that they be forgotten. So his refusal, the tradition says, is an unknowing proof that Joseph lives.

"I will go down to my son mourning, to Sheol". *Sheolah* is the place of the dead, below the earth. The KJV's "the grave" and the BBE's "underworld" both capture a side; Rashi gives the plain sense as the grave and the Midrash as Gehenna; Ibn Ezra takes *sheolah* as "the grave" and criticises an unnamed translator for rendering it Gehenna. In the packet Onkelos reads simply "to Sheol" and Pseudo-Jonathan "to the house of burial". The verb *ered*, "I will go down", picks up *horid* of v. 25 (Joseph taken down) and anticipates the descent of the family to Egypt. The last clause, "and his father wept for him", is ambiguous: Rashi, from the Midrash, says "his father" is Isaac, who wept for Jacob's grief, though he knew Joseph lived; Ibn Ezra reports that the ancients applied the phrase to Isaac, and confirms that Isaac was in fact still alive, since he did not die until Joseph was twenty-nine; Radak computes the same. The plain sense is Jacob himself, named from Joseph's point of view, "his father".

philological_notes.note: "To Sheol": the realm of the dead, with the directional ending. Rashi: plainly the grave, though the Midrash says Gehenna. Ibn Ezra takes it as the grave and criticises an unnamed translator who rendered it Gehenna. In the packet Onkelos reads "to Sheol" and Pseudo-Jonathan "to the house of burial".

"And his father wept for him": 'his father' is Jacob on the plain reading; the Midrash (Rashi) makes it Isaac, as does Pseudo-Jonathan. Ibn Ezra reports that the ancients applied it to Isaac and confirms that Isaac was still alive, not dying until Joseph was 29; Radak makes the same calculation (Isaac died twelve years after the sale).

verses.translation_literal: And the Medanites sold him into Egypt, to Potiphar, an official of Pharaoh, chief of the slaughterers.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the Medanites sold him in Egypt, to Potiphar, an official of Pharaoh, the chief of the slaughterers.
verses.directors_commentary:
The chapter ends by changing the scene and the title. In Canaan the father mourns; in Egypt the boy is for sale. The name here is *Medanim*, not *Midyanim* as in v. 28, and the commentators merge them: Rashbam says Medan and Midian were brothers, sons of Keturah (Gen 25:2), and the two names, with "Ishmaelites", refer to one caravan in the plain sense; Radak adds Judges 8:24. The KJV and ASV simply read "Midianites", harmonising the two spellings; YLT keeps "Medanites".

Potiphar is an Egyptian name, usually taken as "he whom Re has given" (my background knowledge). His title *saris Par'oh*, "official of Pharaoh", uses the word that elsewhere means "eunuch" (YLT keeps this); but Potiphar is married (39:7), so it is best read as "court official". *Sar hattabbachim* is literally "chief of the slaughterers": Rashi takes it as the king's butchers, Onkelos, Ibn Ezra and Ramban as the executioners, with the prison in his house (hence 40:3). The KJV's "captain of the guard" is the later function, not the Hebrew. After the long middle of the chapter, with its dreams, its pit and its lie, the last verse says nothing about how Joseph felt: it records only the sale, the buyer and the title. That silence is what the next chapter fills.

philological_notes.note: "The Medanites": Medan, son of Keturah (Gen 25:2), brother of Midian. Rashbam and Radak take Medan, Midian and the Ishmaelites as one caravan. The same verse differs from v. 28 in the spelling.
"Chief of the slaughterers": Rashi, the king's butchers; Onkelos, Ibn Ezra and Ramban, executioners, since the prison was in his house. The KJV's 'captain of the guard' is a later function.

events.title: Joseph, seventeen, shepherds with his brothers and is favoured
events.narrative_summary: Jacob settles in Canaan. Joseph, aged seventeen, shepherds with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah and brings their bad report to Jacob. Jacob loves him most and makes him a long coat, and his brothers hate him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: v2 gives Joseph's age as seventeen: 17 years from anchor.joseph_birth, margin one year since an age covers a whole year (REGNAL_YEAR). The duration of six months is a convention for the ongoing situation (shepherding, the coat, the growing hatred) which the next scenes follow; v1 is framing for the same setting. The anchor itself is MACRO_ERA (+/-220 years), so every date in the chapter inherits that uncertainty.
events.ancient_year_marker: When he was seventeen years old

events.title: Joseph tells his brothers the dream of the bowing sheaves
events.narrative_summary: Joseph dreams that the brothers' sheaves bow to his. He tells them, and they ask if he will reign over them, and hate him still more.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Text gives no interval. Anchored at the end of the setting scene with no delay, margin two months because the dream falls somewhere within this period of Joseph's seventeenth year. Margin does not move the start. The sheaf scene implies harvest time inside the dream, not at the telling. Tier REGNAL_YEAR: the text counts no days; the gaps are estimates inside Joseph's seventeenth year (v2).

events.title: Joseph tells of the sun, moon and eleven stars, and Jacob rebukes him
events.narrative_summary: Joseph dreams again that the sun, moon and eleven stars bow to him. He tells his father and brothers; Jacob rebukes him, the brothers are jealous, and Jacob keeps the matter in mind.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'He dreamed yet another dream' (v9) after the brothers' reaction to the first: a short gap, here two weeks, give or take two weeks. The telling to his father and brothers is one sitting (v10). Tier REGNAL_YEAR: the text counts no days; the gaps are estimates inside Joseph's seventeenth year (v2).

events.title: The brothers take Jacob's flock to Shechem
events.narrative_summary: Joseph's brothers go to pasture their father's flock at Shechem.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time indication in v12. Placed about two months after the dreams (margin two months) so that the favouritism and dreams are well established. The text does not say where the brothers set out from. Jacob lives in the valley of Hebron (v14), so Hebron is the likeliest starting point and I took it: uv run urim travel loc.hebron_valley loc.shechem: about 98 km by road (78 km straight); a flock moves at the baggage pace, mode army, 3 km/h, 32.7 h moving, about 18 km a day, elapsed about 5 days (a lone walker would need 3). Duration therefore 5 days; the stay at Shechem runs on and is bounded by v17 ('they have departed'). If they were already pasturing elsewhere in the hill country the move would be shorter. Jacob's sending Joseph (a week after, offset kept) still follows the arrival. Tier REGNAL_YEAR: the text counts no days; the gaps are estimates inside Joseph's seventeenth year (v2).

events.title: Jacob sends Joseph from Hebron to check on his brothers
events.narrative_summary: Israel tells Joseph that his brothers are pasturing at Shechem and sends him to see how they and the flock are, and to bring word back. Joseph answers 'Here am I'.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Jacob speaks when the brothers are already at Shechem, so after their arrival; a week later give or take five days is an estimate. Hebron valley is the sending point (v14). Tier REGNAL_YEAR: the text counts no days; the gaps are estimates inside Joseph's seventeenth year (v2).

events.title: Joseph walks from the Hebron valley to Shechem
events.narrative_summary: Joseph sets out from the valley of Hebron and arrives at Shechem.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: uv run urim travel loc.hebron_valley loc.shechem: about 98 km by road, 78 km straight; walking 4 km/h, 24.5 h moving, about 28 km a day: elapsed about 3 days. The text states no duration and a lone traveller walks. Starts immediately on being sent.

events.title: A man finds Joseph wandering and tells him the brothers went to Dothan
events.narrative_summary: A man finds Joseph wandering in the field and asks what he seeks. Joseph asks where his brothers are; the man says they left for Dothan.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows Joseph's arrival at Shechem (v14) as he searches; the exchange takes minutes, one hour allowed with margin of two hours for the searching.

events.title: Joseph follows his brothers to Dothan
events.narrative_summary: Joseph goes after his brothers and finds them at Dothan.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: uv run urim travel loc.shechem loc.dothan: about 28 km by road (23 km straight); walking, 7.1 h moving: elapsed about 1 day. Starts right after the man's directions.

events.title: The brothers plot to kill Joseph as he approaches
events.narrative_summary: The brothers see Joseph from afar and, before he reaches them, plot to kill him and throw him into a pit, saying a wild beast ate him, to see what becomes of his dreams.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: They see him 'from a distance, before he drew near' (v18), and v23 has Joseph arrive after Reuben's speech (vv. 21-22), so the plot starts before his arrival. Anchored on the START of joseph_travels_to_dothan (duration 1 day) with offset 1415 minutes = 23 h 35 min, i.e. the sighting is 25 minutes before the walk ends. The plot (15 min) and Reuben's answer (10 min) then end exactly as Joseph reaches them, and the stripping at v23 follows. 25 minutes is an estimate of how far off a man in open country is seen (a few km at walking pace); margin 10 minutes. Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is given; vv. 18-31 are one day at Dothan and the hours come from estimated durations.

events.title: Reuben persuades them to throw Joseph into a pit rather than kill him
events.narrative_summary: Reuben hears and rescues Joseph from their hands, saying not to take his life. He tells them to throw him into the pit in the wilderness without laying a hand on him, intending to return him to his father.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Immediate response in the same conversation as the plot (v21). Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is given; vv. 18-31 are one day at Dothan and the hours come from estimated durations.

events.title: The brothers strip Joseph of his coat and throw him into a dry pit
events.narrative_summary: When Joseph reaches them they strip him of his long coat, take him and throw him into an empty pit with no water.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'When Joseph came to his brothers' (v23): immediately after Reuben's speech, as the conspiracy's first act. Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is given; vv. 18-31 are one day at Dothan and the hours come from estimated durations.

events.title: While eating, the brothers see a caravan and Judah proposes selling Joseph
events.narrative_summary: The brothers sit down to eat and see an Ishmaelite caravan from Gilead carrying spices to Egypt. Judah proposes selling Joseph to them rather than killing him, and the brothers agree.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: They sit to eat after throwing him in (v25); the caravan's approach and Judah's speech occupy about an hour; margin two hours. Reuben is not present (see v29). Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is given; vv. 18-31 are one day at Dothan and the hours come from estimated durations.

events.title: Joseph is drawn from the pit and sold to the Ishmaelites
events.narrative_summary: Midianite traders pass by. Joseph is drawn up out of the pit and sold to the Ishmaelites for twenty of silver (twenty shekels' weight), and they take him to Egypt. The verbs are unmarked third-person plural, so the text does not say who sells.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the agreement (v27): the traders pass and the sale happens within hours. The text's 'they' in v28 is ambiguous between the brothers and the Midianites (see reviewer note). The journey to Egypt is dated in the last event. Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is given; vv. 18-31 are one day at Dothan and the hours come from estimated durations.

events.title: Reuben finds the pit empty and tears his clothes
events.narrative_summary: Reuben returns to the pit, finds Joseph gone and tears his clothes. He tells his brothers the boy is gone and asks where he can go.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Reuben was absent during the sale. Three hours later, give or take three hours, is an estimate of how long he was away. Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is given; vv. 18-31 are one day at Dothan and the hours come from estimated durations.

events.title: The brothers dip Joseph's coat in he-goat's blood
events.narrative_summary: They take Joseph's coat, slaughter a male goat and dip the coat in the blood.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows Reuben's report with no stated gap. Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: no hour is given; vv. 18-31 are one day at Dothan and the hours come from estimated durations.

events.title: The brothers send the coat to Jacob, who concludes a beast killed Joseph
events.narrative_summary: They send the coat to their father with the words 'This we found; is it your son's?' Jacob recognizes it and says an evil beast has devoured Joseph.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'They sent' (v32) the coat: a messenger travels from Dothan to Hebron. uv run urim travel loc.dothan loc.hebron_valley: about 125 km by road; hurry 5 km/h, 24.9 h moving, about 50 km a day, elapsed about 2 days (walking would take 4 days). Offset 2 days with margin 2 days. Whether Jacob was at Hebron is from v14.

events.title: Jacob mourns Joseph and refuses comfort
events.narrative_summary: Jacob tears his clothes, puts sackcloth on his loins and mourns for his son many days. His sons and daughters try to comfort him but he refuses, saying he will go down to Sheol mourning.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text says 'many days' (v34) and gives no number. Starts the day Jacob sees the coat (offset 0 from the end of the showing), DAY_SEQUENCE since no year is named. The acute mourning is taken as about two months; the real span is weeks to months and cannot be pinned. Rashi (v34) counts 22 years of Joseph's absence, running to Jacob's descent into Egypt, which the anchor chain already dates (Joseph 39); that is not this event. The lasting grief of v35 ('I will go down to Sheol mourning') is a state for the ontologist.

events.title: The Midianites sell Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar
events.narrative_summary: The Midianites (Medanites) sell Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an official of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Anchored on the sale in v28. uv run urim travel loc.dothan loc.egypt: about 565 km by road, 452 km straight; at the donkey rate 32 km/day, 141 h moving, about 17 days; a laden caravan of camels fits that, army-with-baggage pace would give 31 days, hence margin 8 days. Verse 36 is the narrator's anticipation of Gen 39:1.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: The plan to report that a wild beast ate Joseph (chayyah ra'ah, 'an evil beast', 37:20) is the model for the staged evidence in 37:31; the brothers never speak the story to Jacob, who draws the conclusion himself (37:33), so the link is inferred.
Reuben hears the plan to kill Joseph and steps in to rescue him (37:21).
Jacob sends Joseph because the brothers are pasturing at Shechem (37:13).
The bloodied coat is sent to Jacob as proof (37:32).
